passage:
Saturday
Hrithik bhaiya and Arush bhaiya were playing cricket on the terrace again. I asked to play. Hrithik said, "You can be the fielder who fetches the ball." That's not playing! That's being a servant!
Then they made a secret club with a password and wouldn't tell me. Arush said I'm too small to understand.
I told Mamma it was unfair. She said, "Teju, they're older, let them be." Nobody listens to me because I'm the youngest girl. I can bowl better than Arush, actually. I just want them to say, "Teju, you're good, come play properly."
Tejaswini

qa.a: Teju would feel included and respected, and the brothers might discover she really can bowl well. 🙂

passage: Behind the house in the small town of Dharwad, Sunaina and her friends were playing hopscotch with chalk squares on the road. Nandini, seven, stood at the edge with her own chalk. "Can I play, akka?" Sunaina, eleven, didn't even look. "You'll mess it up. Go draw." The big girls laughed. Nandini drew a small square alone and hopped in it, again and again. When Appa came home, she ran to him. "Akka never lets me play! It's not fair!" "She's older, she has her own friends," Appa said, patting her head. Nandini went quiet. She didn't want a pat. She wanted Sunaina to say, "Come, Nandu, your turn."

passage:
Manjula, you're sulking because your cousins won't let you play their card game? Your Neelam dadi knows exactly how that feels.

I was the youngest of four. My sisters and brother always had games I wasn't allowed in. "You're too small." "You don't know the rules." When they did let me play, I was always the thief, never the police.

I used to shout, "It's not fair!" and they'd laugh, which made it worse. I didn't want to be tolerated. I wanted them to look at me like I mattered.

The turning point came one summer when my eldest sister, Kamla, broke her arm. She couldn't play, so she taught me the rules properly, all of them. The next day, I beat my brother.

He never called me small again.

qa.q: How many siblings did Neelam have?
qa.a: Three; she was the youngest of four.

qa.q: What did young Neelam really want from her older siblings?
qa.a: She wanted to be taken seriously and looked up to, not just tolerated, and felt left out and hurt.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Neelam dadi's story?
qa.a: When Kamla, with a broken arm, taught her the rules properly, and she beat her brother the next day.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt teaching her youngest sister?
qa.a: She may have felt bored and restless with a broken arm, and then pleased and proud when Neelam won.

grounding: Neelam dadi recalls being the bossed, left-out youngest who wanted to be taken seriously, and the turning point when a sister taught her properly.

passage:
The school bus had broken down, and all three siblings had to wait at the stop in the drizzle for forty minutes.

Hiba and Arif, the older two, stood under the tin roof playing a word game. Noor, the youngest, tried to join.

"Can I play?"

"You won't get it," said Hiba.

"I will! Tell me the rules!"

"Just watch, Noor."

Noor stood half in the rain, watching. When she shouted out an answer, Arif said, "That doesn't count. You're not playing."

"That's not fair!"

"Life's not fair," said Hiba, and they both laughed.

Noor kicked a puddle. She didn't want them to be nice to her. She wanted them to think she was good at something.

qa.q: How long did they wait at the stop?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What did Noor really want from Hiba and Arif?
qa.a: She wanted to be taken seriously and seen as good at something, not just tolerated, and felt left out and bossed.

qa.q: What could Hiba and Arif do to include Noor?
qa.a: Explain the rules and let her play properly, so she feels respected rather than pushed aside.

qa.q: How do Hiba and Arif seem to see Noor?
qa.a: They seem to see her as too young to understand, not realising how much she wants to be included.

grounding: Stuck at a bus stop, the youngest, Noor, is bossed and left out of her older siblings' game, wanting to be taken seriously, not merely tolerated.

subtype: Stage 4: The middle child's or younger one's view [Receiver]
passage:
Reena was the youngest in their house in Jaipur, and her older brothers, Sonu and Yogi, had a secret club in the storeroom. A sign on the door said NO GIRLS, NO BABIES.

"I'm not a baby!" Reena shouted through the door.

"You're seven!" Sonu shouted back.

She sat outside, arms folded. When they came out, she asked, "Can I carry the torch next time?"

"Maybe," said Yogi, which meant no.

At dinner she complained to Papa. "They never let me in! It's not fair!"

Papa said, "Boys, let her in sometimes."

"Fine," Sonu sighed. "She can sit in the corner."

Reena didn't want to sit in the corner. She wanted to be the one holding the torch.

qa.q: What did the sign on the storeroom door say?
qa.a: NO GIRLS, NO BABIES.

qa.q: What did Reena mean by wanting to hold the torch?
qa.a: She wanted to be taken seriously and given a real role, not just tolerated in the corner; she felt left out and bossed.

qa.q: How could Papa help more than "let her in sometimes"?
qa.a: He could suggest the brothers give Reena a real job in the club, like holding the torch, so she feels valued.

qa.q: How might Sonu and Yogi see their club?
qa.a: They probably see it as their own special space and Reena as too young, not noticing how excluded she feels.

grounding: Reena, the youngest, is bossed and left out of her brothers' club and wants to be taken seriously, not merely tolerated in a corner.

"Can I play?" Leela stood at the terrace door with her own skipping rope.
"No, Leela, it's a big-kids' game," Lavanya said. "You'll just mess it up."
"I won't! I know the rules!"
Nakul laughed. "You can be the umpire. Sit there and don't talk."
"That's not playing. That's sitting!"
"Then go play with your dolls," said Lavanya.
Leela stamped downstairs. "Amma, they never let me play! It's not fair!"
Amma looked up from the vegetables. "What did they say?"
"That I'm a baby. I'm seven! I can count faster than Nakul!"
"You want them to take you seriously."
Leela nodded hard, her eyes full. "I want them to say 'come on, Leela' like they say to each other."
Amma put down the knife. "Let's go up together and ask which job in the game you'd really like."

qa.q: What did Nakul say Leela could be?
qa.a: He said Leela could be the umpire and should sit there and not talk.

qa.q: What does Leela want most when she complains to Amma?
qa.a: Leela feels left out and belittled, and wants the older ones to take her seriously and include her like one of them.

qa.q: How is Amma helping at this point?
qa.a: Amma listens, names that Leela wants to be taken seriously, and offers to go up together to find a real role in the game.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see having Leela in the game?
qa.a: Lavanya seems to see Leela as too little and worries the game will get messed up, without noticing how hurt Leela feels.

grounding: Shows a younger sibling bossed and left out of the older ones' games, protesting unfairness because she wants to be taken seriously.
